faq_a1: Entropy measures password unpredictability in bits. More bits mean more combinations an attacker must try. A password with 80 bits of entropy requires 2^80 attempts — about a quintillion combinations.
faq_a2: Brute-force tries every possible character combination. Modern GPUs can check billions of hashes per second. Our service models an attack at 1 billion guesses/sec.
faq_a3: A dictionary attack uses lists of common passwords from real breaches. Databases like RockYou contain millions of passwords. If yours is in such a list, it will be cracked in seconds.
faq_a4: A password manager generates and stores unique complex passwords for every service. You only need to remember one master password. This solves the password reuse problem.
faq_a5: 2FA adds a second layer of protection: besides a password, you confirm login with a code from SMS, an app (TOTP), or a physical key (FIDO2). Even if the password is stolen, the account stays protected.
faq_a6: Passkeys are a modern password replacement based on public-key cryptography (FIDO2/WebAuthn). Login uses device biometrics or PIN. Passkeys cannot be phished.
faq_a7: NIST recommends: minimum 8 characters (15+ is better), checking against breach lists, banning sequences and repetitions, and NOT requiring mandatory password changes without cause.
faq_a8: Rainbow tables are precomputed hash tables for fast reverse password lookup. Defense: using a salt (random addition) during hashing makes rainbow tables useless.
footer_text: Remember passwords as phrases, add rare characters, and use a password manager — that way you keep both convenience and security.
